topic.title: Osmosis, plasmolysis and turgidity
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Osmosis is asked every year, in two places. On the B2 paper it is a whole question of about 6 to 8 marks: Summer 2024 Higher Q3 gave [2] for choosing the right description and explanation from two lists, [2] for describing and explaining a change in liquid level, [2] for the vacuole and the cytoplasm and [1] for the cell membrane. In Unit 7 it is Prescribed Practical B5 itself — Summer 2025's Booklet A task was potato and parsnip cylinders in sucrose, with percentage changes in mass to one decimal place, the variables table and turgid or plasmolysed cells.
mustMemorise: Osmosis: water molecules diffuse across a selectively permeable membrane, out of the dilute solution and into the one that is more concentrated
Turgid: the vacuole is full and pushes the membrane against the cell wall
Flaccid: the vacuole has shrunk and no longer pushes on the wall
Plasmolysed: the cell membrane has pulled away from the cell wall
The cell wall limits the entry of water, so plant cells do not burst
Percentage change in mass = change in mass ÷ mass at the start × 100
notOnThisSpec: Water potential, solute potential and pressure potential
The words hypotonic, hypertonic and isotonic
Active transport of water (water never moves by active transport)
Transpiration and the potometer, which are the next topic

mustKnow: Osmosis: water diffuses across a selectively permeable membrane, out of the dilute solution and into the more concentrated one
Percentage change in mass = change in mass ÷ mass at the start × 100
Turgid: membrane pressed on the wall; plasmolysed: membrane pulled away from the wall
The cell wall limits the entry of water

mustBeAbleTo: Give the definition of osmosis in the specification's own words, including 'selectively permeable membrane'
Say which way water moves in any situation you are given, and why
Name a cell as turgid or plasmolysed from a drawing, and give the features that show it
Describe what happens to the vacuole, the cytoplasm and the cell membrane as a cell loses water
Explain that the cell wall limits the entry of water, so a plant cell does not burst
Say what happens to an animal cell in pure water and in a concentrated solution, and why it differs from a plant cell
Calculate a percentage change in mass to one decimal place, with its + or − sign
Read the concentration of no change from a graph of percentage change against concentration
Explain a result from Prescribed Practical B5 in terms of the concentrations on either side of the membrane
Say what happens with equal concentrations inside and outside (no net movement), and read it as the zero of the graph
Explain the results of weighed Visking bags in a range of outside concentrations
sheet.howExamined: B2, 1 hour 15 minutes: 70 marks at Foundation, 80 at Higher, calculator allowed. Osmosis usually opens a question with a diagram of an apparatus or a set of cells, then asks for a calculation and an explanation. Marks are single [1] lines with tight accept lists — 'plasmolysed' not 'shrunk', 'pulled away from the cell wall' not 'the wall moved'. The same content is Prescribed Practical B5, so it also appears in Unit 7 Booklet A as a task and in Booklet B as a written question about technique, variables and percentage change. Summer 2026 Higher Booklet B Q4 weighed four Visking bags of one solution in four outside concentrations and asked why a percentage, why one bag lost mass and what the inside concentration could be.
traps: Giving the general definition of osmosis when the question asks about this apparatus (Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q3)
Describing the concentration when the question asks about the level (Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q3)
Avoiding the word 'smaller' twice, for the vacuole and then the cytoplasm, and losing the second mark (Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q3)
Saying the cell wall moved away from the membrane, rather than the membrane away from the wall
Leaving the + or − off a change in mass (Summer 2025 Unit 7 Biology Booklet A)
Writing a percentage change as a whole number when one decimal place was asked for (Summer 2025 Unit 7 Biology Booklet A Higher)
Dividing the change in mass by the final mass instead of the starting mass
Saying sucrose passed through the membrane (Summer 2025 Unit 7 Biology Booklet A Foundation)
Confusing turgor with plasmolysis (Summer 2025 Unit 7 Biology Booklet A Higher)
Leaving the cell wall out of the answer to why a plant cell does not burst (Summer 2023 Unit 7 Biology Booklet B Higher Q4)
Writing a whole-number percentage change as 13 when the column asks for one decimal place: 13.0 is the answer, and the zero carries the mark (Summer 2025 Unit 7 Biology Booklet A Higher Q1)

Explaining a shrunken cell by saying the sucrose solution passed through the membrane: the membrane is selectively permeable, and what moves is water, out of the cell and into the stronger solution (Summer 2025 Unit 7 Biology Booklet A Foundation Q1)

workedExamples.stem:
A carrot cylinder had a mass of 4.40 g. It was left in a 0.8 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution for 24 hours, blotted dry and weighed again. Its mass was then 3.85 g.
(a) Calculate the percentage change in mass. Give your answer to one decimal place. [2]
(b) Explain, in terms of osmosis, why the mass changed. [3]

steps.decision: Final mass minus starting mass, in that order, so the sign comes out right. The minus sign is part of the answer: it says the cylinder lost mass.
Divide by the mass at the START, never the final mass. Percentage change always compares the change with what you began with.

options: Because a percentage change is always measured against the starting value
Because the starting mass is the larger of the two numbers
Because the question gives the starting mass first
whyMenu.explain: The starting value is the reference. Dividing by the final mass gives a different number and loses the mark.

steps.working: The sucrose solution outside is more concentrated than the cell sap inside the carrot cells.
steps.decision: Say which side is more concentrated first. That is the fact the rest of the answer hangs on.

steps.working: So water moved out of the cells, through their selectively permeable membranes, into the solution.
steps.decision: Name the direction and the membrane. A general definition of osmosis with no direction earns nothing here.

steps.working: The cells lost water, became flaccid and then plasmolysed, so the cylinder lost mass.
steps.decision: Finish on the thing the question asked about: the mass. Tie the cell change to the reading.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) −12.5%  (b) The sucrose solution was more concentrated than the cell sap, so water moved out of the cells through their selectively permeable membranes into the solution; the cells lost water and the cylinder lost mass.

steps.decision: One word, spelled properly. 'Shrunk' and 'flaccid' are different answers: flaccid is B, where the membrane still touches the wall.

steps.working: The cell membrane has pulled away from the cell wall.
steps.decision: This is the sentence CCEA wants, and 2024's candidates found it the hardest part of the question. The membrane moves; the wall does not.

steps.working: The solution outside was more concentrated than the cell sap, so water left the vacuole and cytoplasm by osmosis.
steps.decision: Direction first, then the process. Both the vacuole and the cytoplasm get smaller — writing 'smaller' twice is allowed, and it is worth two marks on the real paper.

steps.working: The cell contents shrank, so the membrane could no longer press on the wall and came away from it.
steps.decision: Close the loop: losing water is the cause, the membrane pulling away is the effect.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: C is plasmolysed. The cell membrane has pulled away from the cell wall, because the solution outside was more concentrated than the cell sap, so water left the vacuole and cytoplasm by osmosis and the contents shrank.

workedExamples.stem: A potato cylinder in 10 per cent sucrose solution has a mass of 3.40 g at the start and 3.13 g after 24 hours. (a) Give the change in mass with its sign. [1] (b) Work out the percentage change in its mass, correct to 1 decimal place. [2] (c) Why do students work out a percentage change rather than give the change in grams? [1]

steps.decision: Final minus start; the minus sign records a loss and is a mark of its own in Booklet A.
Divide by the mass at the start, the cylinder's own size.

options: Because the change is compared with the size the cylinder started at
Because the final mass is the more accurate reading
whyMenu.explain: A percentage change compares the change with the starting size. Dividing by the final mass gives a different answer, the slip examiners mark wrong.

steps.decision: One decimal place, and the sign kept.

steps.working: (c) The cylinders started with different masses, so a percentage lets their changes be compared.
steps.decision: The same change in grams means more for a small cylinder than for a large one.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) −0.27 g (b) −7.9 per cent (c) the starting masses differed.

steps.decision: The membrane has come away from the wall, which is what plasmolysed means.

steps.working: (b) The cell membrane has pulled away from the cell wall, and the vacuole is small.
steps.decision: Two separate features, each a mark.

steps.working: (c) Water moves into the cells, across the selectively permeable cell membrane,
steps.decision: Direction first, then the membrane named with its property.

options: Because the cell sap is now more concentrated than the pure water outside
Because sucrose leaves the cells into the water
Because the cell wall pumps water in
whyMenu.explain: In pure water the sap is the stronger solution, so water moves in by osmosis. Sucrose does not cross the membrane, and the wall does no pumping.

steps.working: from the dilute water to the more concentrated cell sap, so the vacuole swells and the cells become turgid.
steps.decision: Dilute to concentrated earns the last mark; the result shows where it leads.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) plasmolysed (b) membrane pulled away from the wall; small vacuole (c) water enters across the selectively permeable membrane from dilute to concentrated; the cells become turgid.

twin.stem: A cell like the one in the diagram is left in pure water for an hour. Which term describes it afterwards?

options.feedback: Water enters, the vacuole swells and the membrane presses back on the wall.
That was its state before; in pure water the sap is the stronger liquid, so water comes back in.
The cell wall limits the entry of water, so a plant cell does not burst.

items.stem: Before we start, three things from B1. Which structure controls what enters and leaves a cell?

options.feedback: The membrane. Everything in this topic happens across it.
The wall is outside the membrane and gives support. The membrane is the one that chooses what crosses.
The vacuole stores cell sap. Controlling entry and exit is the membrane's job.
The nucleus holds the chromosomes and controls the cell's activities, not what crosses its edge.

items.stem: Which structure does a plant cell have that an animal cell does not?

options.feedback: The cell wall — and it turns out to be the reason a plant cell survives being put in pure water.
Both kinds of cell have a membrane. The wall is the plant-only one.
Both respire, so both have mitochondria.
Both have a nucleus. Bacteria are the ones without.

options.text: from where there are more of them to where there are fewer
options.feedback: Down the concentration gradient, with no energy needed. Osmosis is a special case of exactly this.

options.text: from where there are fewer of them to where there are more
options.feedback: That direction needs energy, and it is called active transport. Diffusion goes the other way.

options.text: only when the cell uses energy from respiration
options.feedback: Diffusion is free: it is just molecules moving about at random and spreading out.
Diffusion happens anywhere molecules are free to move, including in air and in liquids with no cell in sight.

items.stem: Complete the sentence. Osmosis moves water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane…
items.skill: State the definition the specification gives

options.text: out of the dilute solution and into the more concentrated one
options.feedback: That is the specification's wording. Water goes to where there is less of it.

options.text: out of the more concentrated solution and into the dilute one
options.feedback: That is the direction the sugar would go if it could fit through. Water moves the other way: towards the more concentrated solution.

options.text: out of the dilute solution and into the more concentrated one, using energy from respiration
options.feedback: The direction is right, but osmosis needs no energy — it is a kind of diffusion. Energy from respiration belongs to active transport.

options.text: between two solutions of equal concentration
options.feedback: Between equal concentrations there is no net movement at all, so nothing would change.

items.stem: A carrot cylinder is left in pure water. What happens to its mass, and why?
items.skill: Predict the direction of water movement

options.text: It increases, because water moves into the cells by osmosis
options.feedback: Pure water is the most dilute solution there is, so water moves into the cell sap.

options.text: It decreases, because water moves out of the cells by osmosis
options.feedback: Water moves towards the more concentrated solution, and that is the cell sap inside the carrot, not the pure water outside.

options.text: It increases, because sugar moves into the cells from the water
options.feedback: There is no sugar in pure water, and sugar molecules are too large to cross the membrane anyway. Only the water moves.

options.text: It stays the same, because the cell wall stops water entering
options.feedback: The wall limits how much water can enter, which is why the cell does not burst, but water does get in and the mass does rise.

items.stem: In a plasmolysed plant cell, which structure has moved?

options.text: the cell membrane, which has pulled away from the cell wall
options.feedback: That is the sentence the scheme wants: the membrane pulls away from the wall.

options.text: the cell wall, which has pulled away from the membrane
options.feedback: The wall is rigid and stays where it is. It is the membrane, with the shrinking contents, that comes away from it.

options.text: the nucleus, which has moved into the vacuole
options.feedback: The nucleus is not what the question is about. Look at the outside of the cell contents: the membrane has left the wall.

options.text: nothing has moved; the whole cell has simply shrunk
options.feedback: The contents shrink, but the wall does not, and the gap that opens between them is the point of the word plasmolysed.

items.stem: A cylinder starts at 4.50 g and finishes at 4.86 g. What is the percentage change in mass?
items.skill: Calculate a percentage change in mass

options.feedback: Change ÷ starting mass × 100 = 0.36 ÷ 4.50 × 100.
That is the change divided by the FINAL mass. A percentage change is always measured against the mass you started with.
That is the change in grams, not a percentage. Divide it by the starting mass and multiply by 100.
Starting mass minus final mass gives the change the wrong way round. The cylinder gained mass here, so the answer is positive.

items.stem: Why does a plant cell in pure water become turgid rather than bursting?
items.skill: Give the role of the cell wall

options.text: The strong cell wall limits how much water can enter
options.feedback: Once the wall is pushed out as far as it will go, no more water can get in. That is the wall's job in this topic.

options.text: The cell membrane stops any more water entering
options.feedback: The membrane is selectively permeable and lets water through freely. It is the wall outside it that limits the entry of water.

options.text: The vacuole stores the extra water safely
options.feedback: The vacuole does fill up, but it is the wall that stops the cell expanding any further and bursting.

options.text: Plant cells do not take in water by osmosis
options.feedback: They do, and that is why they become turgid. What the wall changes is the ending, not the process.

items.stem: A red blood cell is placed in pure water. What happens to it?
items.skill: Contrast an animal cell with a plant cell

options.text: Water enters by osmosis and the cell bursts
options.feedback: An animal cell has no cell wall, so nothing limits the water entering and the membrane splits.

options.text: Water enters by osmosis and the cell becomes turgid
options.feedback: Turgid is a plant-cell word: it needs a wall for the contents to press against. An animal cell simply swells until it bursts.

options.text: Water leaves by osmosis and the cell shrinks
options.feedback: Pure water is more dilute than the cytoplasm, so water moves in, not out. It shrinks in a concentrated solution instead.

options.text: Nothing happens, because the membrane is not permeable to water
options.feedback: The membrane is selectively permeable, and water is exactly the molecule it lets through.

items.stem: A cylinder starts at 5.60 g and finishes at 5.18 g. What is the percentage change in mass?
items.skill: Calculate a signed percentage change from the starting mass

options.feedback: −0.42 ÷ 5.60 × 100 = −7.5, signed for a loss.
That divides by the final mass, 5.18; the divisor is the mass at the start.
That is the change in grams; divide it by the starting mass and multiply by 100.
The cylinder lost mass, so the change is negative.

Osmosis is the diffusion of water molecules from a ______ solution to a more concentrated solution, through a selectively permeable membrane.

accepted: dilute

scheme.for: dilute

parts.workedSolution: Dilute.

commonErrors.feedback: The two words are the right way round for sugar, not for water. Water starts in the dilute solution and moves towards the concentrated one.

parts.stem:
Now the second gap.
Osmosis is the diffusion of water molecules from a dilute solution to a more ______ solution, through a selectively permeable membrane.

accepted: concentrated

scheme.for: concentrated

parts.workedSolution: Concentrated.

commonErrors.feedback: Water finishes in the more concentrated solution, so that is the word for the second gap.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; everything set out in a clear and sensible order; spelling, punctuation and grammar make the meaning clear throughout.

Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; an order you can follow, though it is not held right through; spelling, punctuation and grammar are competent enough for the meaning to be clear.

indicativeContent.point: osmosis moves water across a selectively permeable membrane, out of the dilute solution and into the more concentrated one
the distilled water is more dilute than the cell sap, so water moves into those cells
that cylinder gains mass, and its cells become turgid as the vacuole pushes the membrane against the wall
the cell wall limits the entry of water, so the plant cells do not burst
the sucrose solution is more concentrated than the cell sap, so water moves out of those cells
that cylinder loses mass, and its cells become flaccid and then plasmolysed

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Two cylinders, and for each one: which way the water moves, what happens to the mass, and what happens to the cells.
The two words that separate a Band A answer from a Band B one are turgid and plasmolysed.
parts.workedSolution: Osmosis moves water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane, out of the dilute solution and into the more concentrated one. Distilled water is more dilute than the cell sap of the carrot cells, so water moves into those cells. The cylinder in distilled water therefore gains mass, and its cells become turgid: the vacuole fills and pushes the cytoplasm and membrane against the cell wall. The strong cell wall limits how much water can enter, so the cells do not burst. The 0.8 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution is more concentrated than the cell sap, so water moves out of the cells in the second cylinder. That cylinder loses mass, and its cells become flaccid and then plasmolysed, with the cell membrane pulling away from the cell wall.

commonErrors.feedback: The osmosis is there but the cells are not. Band A needs the state of the cells in both cylinders: turgid in the water, plasmolysed in the sucrose.

prompts.prompt: Define osmosis in the specification's words.
prompts.answer: Water molecules diffuse across a selectively permeable membrane, out of the dilute solution and into the one that is more concentrated.
The vacuole is full of water and pushes the cytoplasm and cell membrane hard against the cell wall.

prompts.prompt: Describe a plasmolysed plant cell, in the words the mark scheme wants.
prompts.answer: The cell membrane has pulled away from the cell wall, because the cell has lost a lot of water.

prompts.prompt: What does the cell wall do when a plant cell is put in pure water?
prompts.answer: It limits the entry of water: once the cell is turgid the wall will not stretch further, so the cell does not burst.

prompts.prompt: Give the equation for percentage change in mass.
prompts.answer: Percentage change in mass = change in mass ÷ mass at the start × 100.

prompts.prompt: A chip of potato is left in very salty water. Say what happens to it and why.
prompts.answer: It loses mass and becomes flaccid: the salty water is more concentrated than the cell sap, so water leaves the cells by osmosis.

prompts.prompt: An animal cell and a plant cell are both put in pure water. How do they end up differently, and why?
prompts.answer: The animal cell bursts because it has no cell wall; the plant cell becomes turgid because its wall limits the entry of water.

prompts.prompt: In Prescribed Practical B5, why is each cylinder blotted dry before its final weighing?
prompts.answer: To remove the solution clinging to the surface, which would otherwise be weighed with the cylinder and make the mass too high.

prompts.prompt: In osmosis, which way does water move?
prompts.answer: From the dilute solution to the more concentrated one.

prompts.prompt: What stops a plant cell in pure water from bursting?

findings.asked: A potato core in a concentrated sugar solution: explain the change in the liquid level and describe the cells.
findings.wentWrong: Many misread the question and wrote about concentration rather than the level; a general definition of osmosis earned nothing - the answer had to say water leaves the potato and where it goes. Some thought 'smaller' could not be used twice (vacuole and cytoplasm both shrink); few could answer about the cell membrane.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Traced the water: from the dilute potato cells, through the partially permeable membranes, into the concentrated solution outside, so the level rises.
findings.rule: Apply osmosis to this situation: which way the water moves and what that does.

findings.asked: Red blood cells in salt solutions of different concentrations; then why potato cells behave differently.
findings.wentWrong: Measuring and picking the matching concentration were fine; the explanation was the most discriminating item on the paper, with many writing the definition or a muddled account, and few linked the potato cell wall to limiting how much water can enter.
findings.rule: Animal cells burst or shrivel; plant cells become turgid or plasmolysed because the wall stops them bursting.

insight.ruleToRemember: Osmosis is the movement of water through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute to a more concentrated solution. In the exam, name the direction for the situation given and its effect (level, mass, length, turgid or plasmolysed); the cell wall is why plant cells do not burst.
insight.aStarSignal: Explaining a novel set-up (Visking tubing, blood cells, potato chips) with the direction of water movement, the reason, and the consequence in one clear chain.
